1:
Ellicott begins by striking a word, since pure is wanting in the best manuscripts, and reads the river simply as full of water that is the emblem of life in its gladness, activity and fulness; he then lines up the prophets who could not describe an age of blessing without a stream, Joel's fountain out of the house of the Lord, Zechariah's living waters from Jerusalem, and Ezekiel's fuller vision still. Barnes fixes the allusion on the first Eden, where a river watered the garden, and marks the one difference that matters, that this water does not spring from the ground but flows from the throne. Henry works the same contrast on a larger scale: what was described before as a city is now described as a paradise, a paradise in a city or a whole city in a paradise, and where the first had two persons to taste its pleasures this second has whole nations. Robertson keeps to the adjective, sparkling like rock crystal. Gill spends his space on refusals, that the river is neither baptism, once administered in rivers and pools, nor the Holy Ghost, whose gifts are elsewhere likened to living water.

Wesley takes precisely the reading Gill has just refused, calling the river the ever fresh and fruitful effluence of the Holy Ghost, and sends the reader to Ezekiel where the trees also bear fruit every month. On the tree itself the grammar is felt to be strained. Clarke argues that since it stands in the streets and on each side of the river the singular must stand for the plural, trees of life rather than one; Wesley says the same in four words, not one tree only. Barnes reports Professor Stuart's quite different construction, which puts the trees between the street and the river in two rows lining the whole stream, but prefers the common reading as giving the more beautiful image, with the tree abounding everywhere. Robertson notes that only one street is mentioned, and that the phrase probably attaches to the river of the previous verse though many attach it to this one. Bede reads the twelve months as intimating the whole time of life, allows that the cross may simply be bearing fruit through the doctrine of the twelve apostles, and makes the leaves a perpetual song, health to those who sing in their now blissful lot.

The removal of the curse is settled partly by text and partly by grammar. Clarke reports that the best manuscripts read not curse but cursed person; Robertson observes that the word has scarcely another example anywhere and may be a syncopated form of the longer term; Ellicott renders it every accursed thing shall not be any longer, hearing a borrowing from Zechariah behind it. Gill takes the curse apart into its cause and its effects, sin on one side and pain, sorrow and death on the other, and finds none of them left. On the promise of seeing his face Robertson gathers the whole biblical thread, that the sight was withheld from Moses, promised to the pure in heart, and held out as possible only to the holy, so that what we now see in the face of Christ becomes at last face to face; he grants the language is anthropomorphic and holds that it touches the essential reality of religion. Wesley adds a curious question of his own about who the subjects of these reigning kings will be, and answers that they are the other inhabitants of the new earth, since a difference must remain between those who excelled and those saved as by fire.
6:
Barnes and Clarke both treat this verse as the seam where the epilogue begins. Barnes lists what has been finished, the enemies quelled, the church triumphant, the affairs of the world wound up and the redeemed received, so that only a few miscellaneous matters remain to close the book; Clarke divides the remainder into three, the angel affirming the truth of what has been spoken, Christ confirming it and pledging himself for the fulfilment, and John warning against adding or diminishing before the apostolic blessing. Henry makes the ratification solemn and wide, confirmed by the name and nature of the God who gave the discoveries, by the messengers chosen, since God would not employ his saints and angels to deceive the world, and by the accomplishment soon to follow; he notes that some extend the words beyond this vision and beyond this book to the completing of the canon itself. Ellicott and Robertson both take the reference to be the whole book rather than the last vision only, Robertson resting the point on the language that follows, which echoes the opening verse. Wesley observes that the conclusion agrees exactly with the introduction.

Whose voice announces the quick coming is a small question with a clear answer. Gill says the words are not the angel's but Christ's, and refuses to take them of the coming in power against Jerusalem, since that was past before John wrote, so that the second and personal coming to judgment must be meant. Barnes agrees they are undoubtedly the Redeemer's though apparently repeated by the angel, and Ellicott allows the same, adding that the Apocalypse is throughout the revelation of the coming One, who came, who comes and is to come. The word quickly is harder, and Robertson meets it by reckoning speed on God's scale rather than ours. Clarke states the difficulty without softening it, that many sayings in this book taken literally would mean the prophecies were to be fulfilled soon after their delivery, which he notes is a strong support for one whole scheme of interpretation. On the beatitude attached to the promise Ellicott puts the weight on a single word, since it is not in reading or wondering or talking but in keeping that the blessing comes, and Wesley says the same while pointing forward to the warning about adding and diminishing.

Ellicott improves the seer's own attestation, reading it as a claim rather than a report, I John am he who hears and sees these things, and hears behind it the opening of the first epistle, that which we have seen and heard declare we unto you — no dream or ingenious fancy of his own but a veritable revelation. Then comes the mistake. Robertson calls the prostration natural though wrong, the more understandable because Christ's own voice had followed the angel's; Barnes thinks John was simply overcome by the extraordinary nature of what he had been shown, and may not improbably have suspected that the Redeemer himself was manifesting himself. Barnes reads the refusal as placing the angel among the prophets, who even at their most eminent were never entitled to worship for the communications they made. Ellicott widens it further, into an affirmation that angels and prophets and simple faithful followers alike stand in one bond of common service to the same Lord. Wesley notices that the words and the reproof are identical with an earlier scene and asks whether this is not the same incident related again, rather than the apostle repeating a fault of which he had been so solemnly warned.
10:
The command not to seal is read against the older prophets. Barnes recalls that Isaiah and Daniel were told to seal their prophecies because these related to far-distant times, the sealing making the record sure and laying it up for future ages so that events might afterwards be compared with it; here the opposite instruction follows from the opposite reason. Ellicott sharpens the contrast into a difference between the dispensations, the one preliminary and prefatory, the other completive and final: however long the gospel age lasts, it is the last time, and after it there is none other. Clarke is blunter and more local, that the sayings are not to be laid up for future generations because they concern the present, and what concerned the Jews was certainly at hand. Robertson notes that John was directed to seal only once in the whole book, and that this one is to be left open for all to read; he also records that Charles takes the speaker to be Christ rather than the angel, and gives his reason for thinking the argument inconclusive. Gill likewise makes it Christ, and observes that the clause is missing from the Ethiopic.

The verse that lets the unjust remain unjust is felt by all of them to need defending. Gill rules out three readings before giving his own, that it is neither irony, nor a permission to do injustice, nor a threat dressed as a licence. Barnes places it firmly beyond the judgment, since no condition this side of the grave is fixed, and finds it proper that at the close of the whole volume of revealed truth the unchangeableness of the final state should be declared in the most solemn manner. Robertson calls the language probably ironical, with the older prophet's words behind it, and in no sense a commendation of the lost estate but a picture of its hopelessness; he adds that Charles rejects the verse as unlike John. Clarke reads it as urgency instead, that fulfilment will come so suddenly there is little space for repentance, so that what is done must be done instantly. Ellicott notes that the four terms are two pairs standing for all classes, those who sin against society and those who sin against themselves, those who act honourably and those who keep themselves pure. Wesley states the consequence flatly.

On the titles that follow Robertson makes the strongest claim in the chapter, that the first of them is applied to God twice in this book and here alone to Christ, which he calls the crowning proof of Christ's deity, and adds that the assurance qualifies him to be the judge just spoken of. Ellicott denies the repetition is rhetorical filling and ties it to what precedes, since men continuing in sin invite against themselves the law by which act ripens into habit, habit makes character and character forms destiny. Then the last beatitude divides the manuscripts. Ellicott reports that two of the best read blessed are they that wash their robes rather than that do his commandments, and prefers it, since it points to a refuge from the very power of sin the warning has described; Robertson reads the same text and notes the verb occurs earlier in the book with the same object. Clarke keeps the received reading and presses the Greek behind right, which he renders authority over the tree of life, founded on obedience and that obedience produced by grace. Wesley recalls that Adam, breaking the commandment, was driven from that tree. Of those left outside, Robertson and Ellicott agree the dogs are not literal but the morally impure, Ellicott explaining that in eastern cities half-wild troops of them scavenged the streets and so became objects of contempt, while Clarke reports the Jewish usage in which the uncircumcised is the dog.
16:
The naming of the speaker is felt as an attestation. Gill sets it beside the seer's own signature, that as John gave his name to what he had witnessed so Christ puts his to what he authored, which is at once a claim on the reader's attention and a declaration of who is speaking of his coming. Robertson calls it the last and most solemn attestation in the book, and insists it is the Jesus of history speaking, who is also the Christ of theology and the Lamb of God. Barnes takes the sending as ratifying and confirming everything communicated by the angel's instrumentality, and reads the address to the churches as reaching the seven directly and immediately and all churches to the end of time remotely; Wesley orders the same chain as the seven angels first, then those churches, then all others in succeeding ages, and Robertson agrees the phrase is not restricted to the seven. Clarke names the sender in three offices at once, maker, redeemer and judge of all men.

The double title takes more explaining, since the same man cannot ordinarily be both root and offspring of another. Barnes gets at it botanically, denying that root means David sprang from him as a tree from a root and making it instead the root-shoot, the sprout that starts up from a fallen or decayed stock. Clarke resolves it by the two natures, root as to the divine, since from him the whole human race sprang and nothing was made without him, and offspring as to the human, taken of the stock of David; he adds the historical point that the whole regal family terminated in Christ, so that as he lives for ever he is the only true and everlasting David. Ellicott puts the paradox in the gospel's own terms, that he is David's Lord and David's Son at once. On the second title Clarke keeps the astronomy working, that as the morning star ushers in the sun so he ushers in the unclouded and eternal glories, and Wesley says the same while reaching back for the star out of Jacob.

Who is calling whom in the last invitation is disputed, and the disagreement is real. Robertson takes the Spirit and the bride to be answering the voice just heard, the Spirit speaking through the prophets joining the people of God in pleading with the Lord Jesus to come, so that the call is directed upward; then he marks the change of person in what follows, where the same verb is applied no longer to Christ but to the thirsty. Ellicott holds both directions together, since the book is the book of the coming One and ends with the cry that he would come, yet those who thirst for his coming are bidden to come to him. Barnes reads the whole verse the other way, as an invitation addressed to men, and argues the construction demands it, finding nothing more appropriate at the close of the volume than that salvation should be announced as free to all. Clarke identifies the callers historically, the prophets and the apostles, the church under the old covenant and the church under the new, and presses the last clause to its limit, that no soul is excluded. Gill locates the Spirit's longing inside believers. Wesley calls it the Spirit of adoption in the bride.
18:
Who utters the closing warning is genuinely disputed. Barnes finds the speaker unnamed and takes the most natural construction to refer it to the writer himself rather than to the angel or the Saviour, reading the whole as John guarding his book against interpolation; he infers that even this early books were liable to corruption by addition or omission, or at least were felt to be. Gill rules that out from the shape of the passage, since the book is not yet finished and both Christ and John speak after this, so the words are neither a copyist's adjuration nor John's own but Christ's. Robertson lays the options side by side and names their holders, Charles rejecting the verses altogether as an interpolation out of harmony with the book, Beckwith taking them for John's own warning drawn from Deuteronomy, and Swete holding them to come from Jesus himself, still bearing witness to the book with a caution against wilful perversion of its teaching. Wesley treats the sanction as reaching further than this book, an awful guard set over the whole New Testament as Moses guarded the law.

What counts as adding and taking away is drawn much wider than copying. Clarke makes adding the giving of any other meaning to the prophecies, or any other application than God intends, and taking away the lessening of the meaning, the curtailing of the sense, the explaining away of the spirit and design; then he applies the warning to himself with unusual candour, confessing that it has weighed on his mind and kept him from indulging his own conjectures about the book or adopting those of others, since the subject is too delicate and awful to trifle with where the meaning is obscure, and he must leave such things to time and event as the surest interpreters. Gill draws the same line at practices rather than manuscripts, counting as subtraction the denying of the book's authority, the withholding of it from the people, and the wilful perverting of its sense so that what it says of antichrist shall not be found to apply. Barnes suggests a motive John may have foreseen, that when the passages describing Antichrist came to be fulfilled, those to whom they applied would be disposed to strike them out or corrupt them.

Henry hears the last exchange as a leave-taking. Christ, having shown these things to his people on earth, seems to part from them and return to heaven, but parts in great kindness and with a promise of speedy return, as at the ascension he parted with a promise of his presence; and to the objection that so many ages have passed since the words were written, Henry answers only that he is not slack. Ellicott marks the emphatic particle that opens the reply, and calls the prophet the mouthpiece of the church whose desire is one with the desire of all who love Christ's appearing; Robertson reads the closing petition as John's absolute belief in the promise just made. Clarke turns the same words on the individual reader, that the Judge is at the door for every person in every age. On the benediction Robertson notes that grace is an unusual close for an apocalypse though suitable for a book meant to be read in the churches, and that saints is John's constant word for believers; Clarke reports that the best manuscripts read all the saints rather than you all, a reading Griesbach admitted as indisputably genuine, and Gill records the same variants from the versions.
